t: #3415 Find Products with Three Consecutive Digits
o: Find product names containing a run of EXACTLY three digits — the digit run must not be part of a longer run (so 'Product56789' with five digits is excluded, while 'ABC123XYZ' qualifies). The robust way is a regular expression requiring a non-digit (or string boundary) on both sides of the three digits: (^|[^0-9])[0-9]{3}($|[^0-9]). Padding the name with sentinel characters avoids explicit boundary alternation.
k: 'Exactly three' means the 3-digit run must be delimited by non-digits or string boundaries on both sides.
Wrapping the name in sentinel characters (e.g., '.') turns boundary checks into plain [^0-9] checks.
MySQL 8's REGEXP_LIKE / REGEXP operator implements this in one predicate.

a.i: Match a 3-digit run preceded and followed by a non-digit or the string start/end, using grouped alternatives for the boundaries.

c.python:
-- MySQL 8+ solution
SELECT product_id, name
FROM products
WHERE name REGEXP '(^|[^0-9])[0-9]{3}($|[^0-9])'
ORDER BY product_id;

a.t: O(total name length) — regex scan per row, linear in name length.

a.i: CONCAT a non-digit sentinel around the name so every real boundary becomes an ordinary character position, simplifying the pattern to [^0-9][0-9]{3}[^0-9] with no alternation.
s: Test REGEXP '[^0-9][0-9]{3}[^0-9]' on the padded string.

c.python:
-- MySQL 8+ solution
SELECT product_id, name
FROM products
WHERE CONCAT('.', name, '.') REGEXP '[^0-9][0-9]{3}[^0-9]'
ORDER BY product_id;

a.t: O(total name length) — same linear regex scan plus O(length) concatenation.

w: Either regex works; the sentinel version is slightly cleaner and avoids dialect quirks around ^/$ in MySQL patterns. The critical trap is writing '[0-9]{3}' alone, which wrongly matches inside longer digit runs like 56789. Test mentally against 'A12B34C' (two separate 2-digit runs → excluded) and '789Product' (digits at the start → included). Follow-up: find names with exactly k digits anywhere, or extract the 3-digit sequences themselves.
